where: Section 3, peripheral clock control (pin configuration sentence)
problem: The advice "Configure unused pins as outputs or with pull-ups disabled, because a floating input can draw current" contradicts its own reason. Disabling the pull-up on an unconnected input is exactly what leaves the pin floating, so the input buffer can sit at mid-rail and draw cross-bar current. A student will follow the sentence and create the current drain it warns about.
fix: Configure every unused pin to a defined level: drive it as an output at a fixed level, or make it an input with the internal pull-up or pull-down enabled (and disable the input buffer where the part allows it). Never leave a pin floating with its pull-up disabled, because a floating input can draw current.

problem: Short-circuit power is said to be "roughly proportional to V² f". The usual model is P_sc ≈ (β/12)(V − 2V_T)³ (t_r + t_f) f, so it grows roughly as V³ f, not V² f. Giving it the same V² f dependence as dynamic power makes the two look identical, which they are not.
fix: Write: short-circuit power is proportional to f and rises very steeply with supply voltage, roughly as (V − 2V_T)³ f, so it is more sensitive to V than dynamic power.

problem: The model P = f³/1000 has hidden units. The number 1000 only works when f is inserted in MHz to get mW; a student who puts f in Hz gets an absurd result and cannot see where the constant came from.
fix: State the model with its units: P(mW) = [f(MHz)]³ / 1000, a numerical fit that assumes V ∝ f and a particular capacitance, used only to show the f³ shape.
